facts.text: On this date in 1989, the Berlin Wall fell — but East Germans didn't storm it. A bureaucrat misread new travel rules live on TV, and confused guards simply stepped aside.
On Nov 9, 1938, Kristallnacht shattered Jewish life across Germany. The night produced so much broken glass that insurance payouts were seized by the Nazi state before victims could collect them.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined — roughly 879,000, holding about 20% of the world's surface fresh water.
Jakarta is sinking up to 25 cm per year in some districts, faster than sea-level rise alone can explain. The culprit is groundwater extraction by residents who lack access to the city's pipe network.
Monaco is denser than any city on Earth — 26,000 people per square kilometer — yet it has one of the world's lowest unemployment rates, sitting below 2%.
On this day in 1998, America Online announced it would acquire Netscape for $4.2 billion — a deal that made the browser war feel won, just as Google was being incorporated in a garage.
On November 9, 1989, the Berlin Wall fell. Within a year, West Germany's DAX index had risen 50%, making reunification one of history's most profitable geopolitical events for equity holders.
The NYSE was founded in 1792 under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street by 24 brokers who agreed to charge each other fixed commissions — a cartel that lasted, more or less intact, for 183 years.
Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO raised $25.6 billion, the largest in history, yet the company sold less than 2% of itself — implying a valuation larger than the entire GDP of Switzerland.
The U.S. penny costs about 3.7 cents to produce. The government has lost money minting its smallest coin every year since 2006, a fiscal irony that Congress has repeatedly chosen to ignore.
On this date in 1934, Carl Sagan was born — the man who calculated there are more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth.
On this date in 1961, NASA announced plans for the Apollo program. The Saturn V rocket it produced remains the most powerful machine ever successfully operated by humans.
Your body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, yet only about 10% of them are human — the rest are bacteria, fungi, and other microbes that outnumber your own DNA.
A neutron star is so dense that a single teaspoon of its matter would weigh about 10 million tons — equivalent to the combined mass of every human who has ever lived.
Light from the Sun takes 8 minutes to reach Earth, but the same photons spent up to 100,000 years fighting their way out from the Sun's core before that final sprint.
On this day in 1989, the Berlin Wall fell — a structure that stood for only 28 years, shorter than the gap between its fall and today.
On this day in 1938, Kristallnacht began. The shards of glass from that night's broken windows were billed to Jewish communities by the Nazi government.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. Oxford dates to 1096; the Aztecs founded Tenochtitlán in 1325.
The fax machine was invented in 1843 — 33 years before the telephone. Alexander Bain patented it while most of the American West was still unmapped.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She died in 30 BC; Khufu's tomb was sealed around 2560 BC.
Saudade (Portuguese): a melancholic longing for something beloved and gone. Linguists consider it untranslatable — the word carries the ache itself, not just its description.
Hiraeth (Welsh): homesickness for a home you cannot return to, or never had. It folds grief, nostalgia, and yearning into a single breath.
On this date in 1989, the Berlin Wall fell — and Germans coined Mauerfall overnight, a compound meaning 'wall-fall,' because German builds new realities by fusing words.
Vellichor: coined by writer John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows — the strange wistfulness of used bookshops. Invented words, if felt widely enough, become real ones.
Sonder: the realization that every passerby lives a life as vivid as your own. Also Koenig's coinage, now appearing in dictionaries — proof that naming a feeling gives it permission to exist.
On this date in 2021, Ethereum's EIP-1559 had already burned over 1 million ETH in its first three months — permanently removing more supply than many entire altcoins ever issued.
On Nov 9, 2022, FTX halted withdrawals after Binance publicly abandoned its acquisition letter of intent, collapsing an $8B hole in roughly 72 hours.
Bitcoin's UTXO model means you never actually 'send bitcoin' — you destroy old outputs and create new ones, including change back to yourself, in a single atomic transaction.
The first real-world Bitcoin purchase — 10,000 BTC for two pizzas in May 2010 — was not a spontaneous act. Laszlo Hanyecz negotiated it on a forum for four days before anyone accepted.
Ethereum's beacon chain ran for 28 months with real staked ETH — over $20B at peak — before the merge, with no way to withdraw. Stakers had no exit until the Shanghai upgrade in April 2023.
On this day in 2016, Google DeepMind's AlphaGo defeated European champion Fan Hui 5-0 — the first time a machine beat a professional Go player without handicap, years ahead of expert predictions.
On this date in 2022, Meta released Galactica, a 120B-parameter science LLM. It was pulled after 72 hours when users found it confidently fabricated citations, dosages, and historical facts.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of about 4,500 average US households.

The first neural network to achieve superhuman performance on ImageNet (AlexNet, 2012) ran on two consumer GTX 580 GPUs with 3GB VRAM each. Modern frontier models require clusters of tens of thousands of far more powerful chips.
Transformers were introduced in a 2017 paper by eight Google Brain and DeepMind researchers. Six of the eight authors have since left Google, several to found competing AI labs.
